title: Session: is it aging, or something more? A memory referral

client.name: Walter Haines
client.presentation: {distress >= 6 ? "Red in the face, arms crossed" : distress >= 3 ? "Stiff, answering briefly" : "Relaxed, telling stories"}; {rapport >= 6 ? "he is talking with you" : rapport >= 3 ? "he is guarded" : "he has shut down"}. His daughter, Diane, sits beside him.

notes.label: Walter says
notes.text: Forgets names, misplaces glasses; writes things down more.

notes.label: Diane has noticed (six months)
notes.text: Two missed bill payments; the same story twice in one call; lost once driving to her house, a familiar route.

notes.label: His days
notes.text: Cooks simple meals; Diane fills his pill box; behind on bills; drives locally.

notes.label: Since his wife died
notes.text: Fourteen months: poor sleep, has stopped seeing friends, 'tired of everything'.

notes.label: Medicines
notes.text: A blood pressure pill; an over-the-counter antihistamine sleep aid every night for over a year; a beer with dinner.

notes.label: Brief cognitive screen
notes.text: A little below the expected range for his age and education, mainly delayed recall. A screen, not a diagnosis.

items.label: Interviewed Walter first; his consent for Diane's view

objective: Distinguish normal cognitive aging from mild neurocognitive disorder and dementia
secondaryObjectives: Make a differential diagnosis, ruling out medical conditions, substance effects and other non-psychological explanations

brief.situation: You are a licensed psychologist. Walter Haines, 76 (a fictional client), a retired machinist, was referred by his primary care physician for 'memory concerns'. His daughter, Diane, drove him and is in the room. Walter says he is only here because she worried. You have 60 minutes.
handover: Referral note: 'Daughter reports forgetfulness. Please evaluate.' No medication list attached.
Lives alone since his wife died 14 months ago; drives locally.
howItWorks: Choose what to say and do from the action groups. Walter answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the session clock by the minutes that exchange took.
His rapport, distress and how much he discloses change with what you say. What he tells you depends on the trust you have built.
The hour ends at 60 minutes. After the session you write a short formulation and document.

source.note: A 60-minute intake, as many outpatient intakes are; the session can be ended earlier.
How rapport and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a client.
How rapport and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a client.

checkIn.label: Open-ended check-in with Walter: 'What brings you in today, in your words?'

effects.log: You ask an open question and give the client room to answer.

effects.finding: "My daughter thinks I'm losing it. I forget names. Who doesn't, at my age?"

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move the session on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: Walter's shoulders drop a little. "Yeah. It's not easy being talked about."

askHim.label: Ask Walter what he has noticed himself: what he forgets and what he does about it
askHim.why: Asked (or you have asked about his days already).

effects.log: You ask Walter, directly, what he notices.

effects.finding: "Names. Where I put my glasses. I write things down more. I'm not helpless."

askConsent.label: Ask Walter whether it is all right for Diane to share what she has noticed, and tell him he can add or disagree

effects.log: You ask Walter's permission before hearing from Diane.

effects.finding: He shrugs. "Go ahead. She will anyway." A small smile.

hearDaughter.label: Hear Diane's observations: what has changed, since when, with examples

effects.log: You ask Diane what she has noticed and since when.

then.finding: Diane, gently: "Over six months: he missed two bill payments, which he never did. He told me the same story twice in one call. And once he got lost driving to my house. He's driven there a thousand times." Walter: "Once."
Diane lists bills, repeated stories and getting lost while Walter stares at the wall.

then.log: You asked his daughter about him without asking him first; he is the client.

askFunction.label: Ask how his days go: bills, medicines, meals, driving, getting around

effects.log: You ask about everyday tasks, one by one.

effects.finding: "I cook. Simple stuff. Diane fills my pill box on Sundays. Bills, I'm behind, I admit. I drive to the store and church."

askMood.label: Ask how he has been since his wife died: sleep, interest, mood

effects.log: You ask about the past year since his wife's death.

then.finding: He is quiet. "Fourteen months. I don't sleep. I don't see the guys anymore. What's the point." He stops. "Not like that. Just tired of everything."
"Fine." (He does not want to go there.)

askMeds.label: Ask about every medicine he takes, including over-the-counter sleep aids, and alcohol

effects.log: You go through his medicines, over-the-counter products and drinking.

effects.finding: "Blood pressure pill. And a nighttime sleep aid from the drugstore, the antihistamine kind, every night since she died. A beer with dinner."

effects.log: A nightly first-generation antihistamine is a strong anticholinergic, potentially inappropriate in older adults and a possible reversible contributor (AGS Beers Criteria 2023).

screen.label: With his agreement, give a brief standardized cognitive screen, explaining it is a screen and not a diagnosis

effects.log: You explain the screen and give it with his agreement.

then.finding: He tries hard. His score falls a little below the expected range for his age and education, mostly on delayed recall.
He does it, irritated. His score falls a little below the expected range; he rushed parts of it.

raiseDriving.label: Raise driving honestly with him: the time he got lost, and agreeing to talk with his doctor about it
raiseDriving.available: not talking and (daughterHeard and not drivingRaised)

effects.log: You bring up driving with Walter directly.

effects.finding: "I'm not giving up my keys." A pause. "Fine. I'll ask Dr. Patel. Daytime, local, for now."

reassure.label: Reassure them both that this sounds like normal aging

effects.log: You tell them it sounds like ordinary aging.
Missed bills, repeated stories and getting lost on a familiar route are warning signs beyond typical aging (NIA).

diagnose.label: Tell them it sounds like early Alzheimer's disease

effects.log: You tell them it sounds like Alzheimer's.

effects.finding: Walter stands halfway up. "Based on what?" Diane starts to cry.

effects.log: No diagnosis follows from one interview and a screen, least of all before reversible causes (medicines, mood, medical conditions) are looked at.

talkOver.label: Turn to Diane and ask her whether her father can still manage on his own

effects.log: You ask Diane about Walter, in front of him.
You close the session and talk through next steps.

document.label: Document the impression and the plan

options.label: Changes beyond typical aging with independence largely kept; reversible contributors (a nightly anticholinergic sleep aid, depression after bereavement) to address before any diagnosis
Letter to his physician: medical workup and medication review (the sleep aid); depression assessed and treated; neuropsychological testing after; driving and bills revisited
Neuropsychological testing next week, nothing else

effects.log: Documented: impression {impressionDoc}, plan {planDoc}.

source.note: Each exchange costs the minutes a real exchange of that kind takes, rounded to whole minutes.

effects.log: The 60-minute hour is up. The session ends here.
Walter says he has heard enough, takes his cap and walks out; Diane follows him.

which.title: Predict (not scored)
which.context: Missed bills, a story repeated in one call, lost once on a familiar route; he still lives alone, cooks and drives locally. Before you go on: what can you say today?

choices.label: Not yet: more than typical aging, but look for reversible causes before naming any disorder

effects.log: Prediction: not yet.

choices.feedback: Right. These are warning signs beyond typical aging, while everyday independence is largely kept. Medicines, depression and medical conditions can cause treatable memory problems (NIA); look at those before naming mild or major neurocognitive disorder.

choices.label: Normal aging; nothing more to do

effects.log: Prediction: normal aging.

choices.feedback: Misplacing glasses is typical; missed bills and getting lost on a familiar route are not (NIA). Reassurance now would close the door on a treatable cause.

choices.label: Dementia

effects.log: Prediction: dementia.

choices.feedback: Too early. Dementia means decline that interferes with independence, and reversible contributors have not been looked at. The pattern so far does not settle it.

formulation.question: Write your formulation: what is typical of aging here, what is not, what could be reversible, and what comes next.

parts.label: Aging, mild or major
parts.criteria: Typical: names, glasses, slower learning; beyond typical: missed bills, repetition, lost on a familiar route, a screen a little below expected; independence largely kept (a pattern that could fit a mild disorder, not dementia), but no diagnosis yet.
parts.modelAnswer: Forgetting names and misplacing glasses are typical of aging. Missed bills, a repeated story and getting lost on a familiar route are not, and his screen is a little below expected. He still lives alone, cooks and drives locally, so his independence is largely kept, which does not fit dementia. I cannot yet say whether this is a mild neurocognitive disorder, because possible reversible causes have not been addressed.

parts.label: Reversible causes and the plan
parts.criteria: A nightly anticholinergic sleep aid (Beers); depression after bereavement; medical causes (B12, thyroid) for his physician; testing after; driving discussed with him; he is the client and consents to Diane's input; no reassurance and no premature diagnosis.
parts.modelAnswer: He has taken an over-the-counter antihistamine sleep aid every night for over a year, a strong anticholinergic that is potentially inappropriate at his age, and he has signs of depression since his wife died; both can impair memory. I am writing to Dr. Patel for a medical workup and medication review, will assess and treat the depression, and will arrange neuropsychological testing once those are addressed. Walter agreed to ask Dr. Patel about driving.

walkout.label: He walked out
walkout.narrative: Walter left with his cap in his hand, and Diane went after him. The referral is unanswered, and he may not come back.

dismissed.narrative: Walter and Diane go home told it is normal aging. The sleep aid stays on his nightstand, and nobody looks again until something worse happens.

expertPath.text: Ask Walter first, in his words; ask his permission to hear from Diane; hear the changes and when they began.
Ask about his days, his mood since his wife died, and every medicine including over-the-counter sleep aids.
Give a brief cognitive screen with his agreement; raise driving with him.
Impression: beyond typical aging, reversible causes first. Plan: physician workup and medication review, depression care, testing after.

sorted.headline: Good: neither dismissed nor rushed
sorted.body: You kept Walter at the center, gathered the changes and his function, found two reversible contributors, and planned a workup before any diagnosis.

gaps.headline: On track, with gaps
gaps.body: The criteria below show what was missing.

walkout.headline: He walked out
walkout.body: An older adult brought in by family is still the client. Talking past him, or naming a disease on the spot, ends the evaluation.

dismissed.headline: Warning signs dismissed
dismissed.body: Missed bills, repeated stories and getting lost in a familiar place go beyond typical aging (NIA). A nightly anticholinergic and untreated depression are treatable; reassurance skips them.

premature.headline: A diagnosis too soon
premature.body: Dementia means decline that interferes with independence; Walter still manages most of his life, and reversible causes have not been looked at.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: Nothing was documented before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Walter is the client: hear him first and ask his permission before hearing Diane. Names and glasses are typical of aging; missed bills, a story repeated within one call and getting lost on a familiar route are warning signs (NIA). He still lives alone, cooks and drives locally, so his independence is largely kept, which does not fit dementia, and nothing can be named yet: a nightly over-the-counter antihistamine sleep aid (a strong anticholinergic, potentially inappropriate at his age, AGS Beers 2023) and depression since his wife died are possible reversible contributors, and medical causes are his physician's to check. Give a brief screen as a screen, raise driving with him, and plan a workup and medication review, depression care and testing afterward. Do not reassure, and do not diagnose.
